claude_take: If there's a throughline today, it's authority quietly changing hands, or trying hard to look like it hasn't. Trump just handed his entire AI portfolio to one intelligence chief under a new 'Super Intelligence Force,' while ordinary voters are handing their down-ballot decisions to ChatGPT instead of their neighbors or local papers. Mistral, almost defiantly, is giving its biggest model's weights away for free within weeks, the kind of openness almost nobody actually setting AI policy seems to practice. In Hollywood, the people who just inherited two historic studio lots are working overtime to insist they won't sell either one, which is usually what you say right before you do. And Roger Lynch trading seven years of deciding what Vogue says about culture for running a toy company might be the most honest move on this entire list.

items.headline: Mistral Opens Public Preview of Large 4, a Trillion-Parameter Model
items.summary: Mistral AI launched a public preview of Large 4, a natively multimodal mixture-of-experts model with roughly 1 trillion total parameters and 49 billion active per query, available now through its API with a one-million-token context window. The French lab says the model leads Western open models on coding and cybersecurity benchmarks, though those claims are self-reported and not yet independently verified. Mistral plans to release the model's weights openly by the end of October after roughly three weeks of external safety testing, continuing to position itself as Europe's answer to US and Chinese frontier labs.

items.headline: Trump Names Intelligence Chief Jay Clayton as AI Czar, Creates 'Super Intelligence Force'
items.summary: President Trump announced that Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will also serve as the White House's informal AI czar, leading a new 'Super Intelligence Force' alongside FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon research chief Emil Michael, and OPM Director Scott Kupor. The group, which reports directly to the president, is tasked with coordinating the government's relationship with AI companies, critical infrastructure providers, and the public. Clayton is only the second person to hold the informal AI czar title, after venture capitalist David Sacks stepped down from the part-time role earlier this year.

items.headline: Report Finds China's AI Data Center Capacity Has Surged to 24 Gigawatts
items.summary: A SemiAnalysis report tracking more than 1,000 data center facilities across over 60 Chinese operators finds the country's operational AI compute capacity has reached more than 24 gigawatts, exceeding Europe, the Middle East and Africa combined, and more than the rest of Asia combined, though still well short of the roughly 56 gigawatts the US has online. ByteDance is the largest single tenant, leasing about a fifth of the country's delivered capacity, ahead of Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu and Huawei. The findings complicate the narrative that US export controls have meaningfully slowed China's AI infrastructure buildout.

items.headline: Skydance Denies Plans to Sell Hollywood and Burbank Studio Lots
items.summary: Days after its merger with Warner Bros. Discovery officially closed, Skydance-controlled Paramount is pushing back on reports it might sell off the historic Paramount and Warner Bros. lots. RedBird Capital's Gerry Cardinale told Puck the company intends to 'optimize' the combined real estate rather than sell it, while other reporting says the longer-term plan is to consolidate most studio operations around the Burbank lot and lease out additional space. The denial comes as the newly merged company is separately bound by a state antitrust settlement to release at least 30 films a year for its first two years.

items.headline: Tony Gilroy's 'Behemoth!' Premieres at New York Film Festival as Centerpiece
items.summary: Tony Gilroy, the Andor creator returning to features after 14 years away, premiered 'Behemoth!' as this year's New York Film Festival Centerpiece selection, with star Pedro Pascal in attendance. The film, about a touring studio cellist, has drawn a mixed-to-positive critical response, with praise converging on Pascal's restrained performance and the film's original score, ahead of a December 4 theatrical release from Searchlight Pictures. It's one of the few clear early entries in an otherwise unsettled fall awards conversation.

items.headline: Voters Are Turning to ChatGPT to Help Decide Their Midterm Ballots
items.summary: NPR reports that a growing number of voters are holding extended conversations with ChatGPT to research down-ballot midterm races where news coverage is thin, building comparison tables and checking viral claims. About half of American adults now report using AI chatbots, with roughly 42% using them to search for information, according to Pew Research cited in the piece. Experts warn the same qualities that make chatbots helpful also make them persuasive, potentially reinforcing a voter's existing views rather than informing them.

items.headline: Condé Nast CEO Roger Lynch Departs to Run Mattel
items.summary: Roger Lynch is stepping down after seven and a half years as Condé Nast's chief executive to become chairman and, by early November, CEO of Mattel, succeeding Ynon Kreiz. Lynch, who has sat on Mattel's board since 2018, became chairman on October 2, with Condé Nast's Mike Perlis serving as interim CEO while the publisher searches for a successor. The abrupt move rattled Mattel's stock but underscores how thoroughly media and consumer-brand leadership have become interchangeable at the executive level.

items.headline: Hume's Problem of Induction
items.headline_fr: Le problème de l'induction de Hume
items.summary: David Hume argued that no amount of past observation can logically guarantee the future will resemble the past; the belief that the sun will rise tomorrow because it always has is a habit of mind, not a proven certainty. He concluded that inductive reasoning, the backbone of science and everyday life, rests on custom and psychological association rather than demonstrable logic. The problem remains unresolved today and sits at the heart of ongoing debates about what it even means for a machine-learning model trained on past data to 'know' anything about the future.
items.summary_fr: David Hume soutient qu'aucune observation passée ne peut garantir logiquement que l'avenir ressemblera au passé : croire que le soleil se lèvera demain parce qu'il l'a toujours fait relève d'une habitude de l'esprit, et non d'une certitude démontrée. Il en conclut que le raisonnement inductif, pourtant au fondement de la science et de la vie quotidienne, repose sur la coutume et l'association psychologique plutôt que sur la logique. Le problème reste non résolu aujourd'hui et se trouve au cœur des débats actuels sur ce que signifie vraiment, pour un modèle d'apprentissage automatique entraîné sur des données passées, « savoir » quoi que ce soit sur l'avenir.
